title: How can twelve sectors give three or four angles of symmetry?
description: A circle cut into twelve equal sectors is coloured so that it has three angles of symmetry, then four. The turn for each is changed into a number of sectors, and the possible numbers of angles are found. The check multiplies the angles by the sectors in each turn.
teaching_notes: One idea: a turn that brings the colouring onto itself is a whole number of sectors, so the colouring repeats every few sectors. Watch for students who colour the sectors without checking the turn.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, second block)
video_script.why: The child colours a twelve-sector circle to get three and four angles of symmetry and finds which numbers of angles are possible.
video_script.substitution: a circle cut into twelve equal sectors, with coloured sectors acting like the radial arms of the book
video_script.anchor: the book's circle cut into twelve equal sectors
video_script.payoff_line: Colour every fourth sector for three angles, and every third sector for four angles

final_answer.value: 3 angles: colour every 4th sector. 4 angles: colour every 3rd sector. Possible numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12
final_answer.spoken: colour every fourth sector for three angles, every third sector for four angles, and the possible numbers are one, two, three, four, six and twelve

maths_rules: 3 angles of symmetry: first turn 120°, 120 ÷ 30 = 4 sectors; colour every 4th sector, 3 sectors coloured
4 angles of symmetry: first turn 90°, 90 ÷ 30 = 3 sectors; colour every 3rd sector, 4 sectors coloured
the colouring can repeat every 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 sectors, which fit a whole number of times into 12
number of angles = 12 ÷ sectors per repeat = 12, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1
video_script.design: The circle with twelve equal sectors, each thirty degrees wide. Coloured sectors are placed every fourth, then every third, and turned to see them land on each other. The sizes that fit twelve give the possible numbers of angles.
open_questions: The book's own answer line reads 12 angles of symmetry are possible; here all the possible numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 are given, the largest of which is 12.

narration: <bookmark mark='full'/>Step one, the circle is one full turn of three hundred sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Three hundred sixty divided by twelve is thirty degrees.
Each sector is thirty degrees wide.

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step two, take three angles of symmetry.
The first turn is one hundred twenty degrees.
<bookmark mark='div'/>One hundred twenty divided by thirty is four sectors.
<bookmark mark='col'/>Colour every fourth sector, and three sectors are coloured.

beats.on_screen: 4 angles: first turn 90°; 90° ÷ 30° = 3 sectors; colour every 3rd sector; 4 sectors coloured

marks.turn: the first turn of 90° is marked on a fresh circle
marks.col: every third sector is coloured teal and each lands on the next when turned

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step three, take four angles of symmetry.
The first turn is ninety degrees.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Ninety divided by thirty is three sectors.
<bookmark mark='col'/>Colour every third sector, and four sectors are coloured.

beats.on_screen: the colouring repeats every k sectors, k fits 12 whole times: k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12; number of angles = 12 ÷ k = 12, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1
narration: <bookmark mark='k'/>Step four, the colouring can repeat every one, two, three, four, six or twelve sectors.
Each size fits a whole number of times into twelve.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Twelve divided by each gives twelve, six, four, three, two or one angle.

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step five, check each pair against the whole circle of twelve sectors.
Three angles of four sectors make twelve.
Four angles of three sectors make twelve.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Twelve of one, six of two, two of six and one of twelve do too.
